extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and formulating rejections under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), including identifying judicial exceptions and explaining why claim elements do or do not amount to significantly more than an exception. Focused on examiner procedures and reasoning to support Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use / technological-environment limitations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of limitations that the courts have described as merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance lists specific examples (i–x) such as limiting drug administration to a particular patient population (Mayo), identifying hedging participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), narrowing a formula to wheels (Flook), specifying execution on a computer (FairWarning), limiting virus screening to telephone/Internet networks (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec), limiting collecting/analyzing/displaying information to electric power grid data (Electric Power Group), informing doctors to apply a law of nature to detect polymorphisms (Genetic Techs.), implementing budgeting via a broad "communication medium" (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One), using advertising-as-currency on the Internet (Ultramercial), and requiring online/computer implementation for guaranteeing transactions (buySAFE). Examiners should treat "technological environment" and "field of use" interchangeably and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP §2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that merely link an exception to a particular environment, explain in the rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should be aware that the courts often use the terms 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of the eligibility analysis, treat these terms interchangeably and consider overlap with Step 2B factors like insignificant extra-solution activity. Evaluate each claim on its own merits and the other Step 2B considerations before deciding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be used when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: For efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The results of the streamlined analysis must always match the full Alice/Mayo analysis; it is not a way to avoid an ineligibility finding. If in doubt whether the applicant seeks coverage for an exception, perform the full analysis. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident when claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception and clearly improves technology or computer functionality may be eligible at Pathway A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a robotic arm assembly with a control system operating using certain mathematical relationships; an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral; products with merely ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact). Do not use streamlined analysis if the claim lacks self-evident eligibility or if it's a close call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology/computer functionality can avoid full analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to clear improvements to computer-related technology or functionality (or other technological processes) may avoid the full eligibility analysis (e.g., Enfish, McRO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are viewed as a whole and their eligibility is self-evident based on a clear improvement, no further analysis is needed. If claims present a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM), perform the full Alice/Mayo test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility rejections must be based on substantive law and judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be based on failure to comply with 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; training materials and examples do not themselves serve as the legal basis for a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may cite training materials or examples in support of an argument, but applicants should not be required to model claims after those examples to attain eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the record as a whole and evaluate claims individually
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a claimed invention for eligibility, examiners should review the record as a whole (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law or prior art) and make eligibility determinations claim-by-claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is ineligible because they may add limitations amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception. Consider each claim separately based on its particular elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirement for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If it's more likely than not that a claim does not satisfy eligibility criteria, examiners should formulate an appropriate rejection that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible clearly and specifically so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond. The rejection should provide clear and specific reasons for ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 rejections must explain why claim is not within a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding a claim does not fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection should explain why the claim is not directed to one of the four statutory categories of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.03(a) for instructions on making such a rejection; provide sufficient clarity and specificity in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites or describes the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it corresponds to concepts the courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(2)). Citing appropriate court decisions that support the identification is a best practice; ensure the cited decision's facts reasonably tie to the present case. Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts match uniquely. Sample explanation provided: 'The claim recites the steps of sorting information by X, which is an abstract idea similar to concepts identified by the courts...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A for laws of nature/natural phenomena/products of nature: identify and provide reasoned rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is determined to recite a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature, the rejection should identify that subject matter as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered such an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explanations for correlations (law of nature), naturally occurring phenomena, or why a product lacks markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart. Sample explanations illustrate comparing isolated products to natural counterparts and assessing marked differences in structure, function, or properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: identify additional elements and explain why they do not amount to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they, individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address both individual elements and the combination; a new combination of known steps may be eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Provide a reasoned explanation—if elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, explain why courts or those in the field would recognize them as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain conventionality when relying on 'well-understood, routine, conventional' findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding certain claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or persons in the relevant field would recognize, those limitations as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion and, where available, use sources of evidence (specification statements, manuals, patents, case law) to support assertions. See MPEP §2106.05(d) for further information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components performing generic functions do not meaningfully limit a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) may be explained as not meaningfully limiting the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §2106.05(d) lists computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically. However, not all computer functions are necessarily conventional; courts have found eligible situations where generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (e.g., DDR Holdings). Explain why the claimed computer functions are generic and do not add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use linking do not add meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data) or generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use may be insufficient to add significantly more to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: storing data added to mathematical computation does not meaningfully limit; employing well-known computer functions to execute an abstract idea, even when limited to a particular environment, may not add significantly more (cf. Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §2106.05(g) for insignificant extra-solution activity and §2106.05(h) for field-of-use linking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: consult the specification to identify elements that could overcome a §101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rejection is made, examiners should consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to a claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggesting claim amendments from the specification is a way to assist applicant in overcoming the rejection and clarifies how the claim could be made eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirements: eligibility is a question of law; evidence not required but may be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider the determination of eligibility to be a question of law and generally do not require evidence to identify a judicial exception or to conclude additional elements are conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While evidence is not required, available evidence can be provided to support assertions or rebut applicant arguments (e.g., specification statements, manuals, patents, court decisions). When citing case law or other evidence, ensure the facts comport with the application under examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B rejections should be readily apparent based on examiner expertise and accompanied by rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under Step 2B should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner, relying on their expertise in the art, that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the underlying rationale in the Office action so the applicant can effectively respond; when appropriate, explain why additional elements instead provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation.
